title: Jailbreak Judge Disagreement Analysis: Which Attacks Fool Automated Evaluators But Not Humans?

original_idea.quick_reasoning: Clearly addresses an AI Safety problem with a reasonably scoped approach.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: judge reliability is described as a crisis in jailbreak evaluation. Understanding failure modes of automated judges directly improves benchmark validity and helps practitioners choose the right evaluator for their threat model.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Running three different evaluators on model responses is primarily scripting and analysis. StrongREJECT provides a ready-to-use evaluator. The main complexity is qualitative analysis of disagreement patterns. Guided beginners can execute.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Scoring 200 responses with 3 judges is manageable, but the human rating component and qualitative analysis of linguistic patterns adds time. The calibrated scoring rubric proposal extends scope beyond a single experiment.

novelty.reasoning: Judge reliability in jailbreak evaluation is actively studied. 'Know Thy Judge' (Eiras et al., ICLR 2025 workshop, arXiv:2503.04474) demonstrates that small output style changes cause up to 0.24 jumps in false negative rates and adversarial attacks can fool judges on 100% of harmful generations. 'A Coin Flip for Safety' (arXiv:2603.06594) directly argues LLM judges fail to reliably measure adversarial robustness. JAILJUDGE (OpenReview) provides a comprehensive jailbreak judge framework. However, the specific analysis of which attack categories produce human-automated disagreement and the qualitative linguistic pattern analysis of disagreement cases adds novel empirical methodology on top of the known problem.
